sections.b: The letter alternates between "some" and "you": the false teachers (1:3-11; 4:1-5; 6:3-10) and Timothy's own charge (1:18-20; 4:6-16; 6:11-16, 20-21). Between them come the instructions for God's household: prayer and worship (chapter 2), overseers and deacons (chapter 3), widows and elders (chapter 5), slaves and the rich (6:1-2, 17-19). Three "trustworthy sayings" (1:15; 3:1; 4:9), a hymn (3:16) and two doxologies (1:17; 6:15-16) give it its high points.

1 Timothy is the longest of the three and the most concerned with church order: it alone has the deacons (3:8-13), the enrolled widows (5:3-16) and the pay and discipline of elders (5:17-22). It shares with Titus the list of qualities for overseers (3:1-7; Titus 1:5-9) and with both letters the vocabulary of "sound teaching," "godliness" and the "appearing" of Christ. Unlike 2 Timothy, it has no farewell tone: Paul expects to come soon (3:14; 4:13).

1 Timothy shows Timothy left at Ephesus with a hard task: to order older and established teachers to stop (1:3), to correct elders (5:19-20), and to be a model though young (4:12). His authority rests on prophecies and the laying on of the elders' hands (1:18; 4:14) and on Paul's letter itself. Paul's advice about water and wine (5:23) is one of the few personal touches.

The main text in the debate. "I do not allow a woman to teach or to hold authority over a man; she is to be in quietness" (2:12) is grounded in the order of creation and in Eve's deception (2:13-14), and followed by the hard saying that "she will be saved through the bearing of children" (2:15). Readers divide over the meaning of authentein, over whether the rule was for one church facing false teaching or for all churches, and over whether 2:13-14 states a principle or gives an illustration. The chapter page sets the readings side by side, and the card there gives each church's position.

common: Most churches that limit ordination to men cite 1 Timothy 2:12 and 3:1-7, alongside the example of the Twelve.
uncommon: Some read 2:12 as "I do not allow a woman to teach that she is the author of man," against a myth that Eve was created first.

sections.b: 1 Timothy speaks of "the overseer" (3:1-7) and of "elders who lead well" (5:17), some of whom labor in preaching and teaching. It gives qualifications for the first and pay and discipline for the second: double honor, charges only on two or three witnesses, public correction for those who keep sinning, and no hasty laying on of hands (5:17-22). Timothy himself received his gift through the laying on of the elders' hands (4:14). Whether "overseer" and "elder" are one office here, as they seem to be in Titus 1:5-7, is debated.
sections.refs: 1 Timothy 3:1-7; 1 Timothy 4:14; 1 Timothy 5:17-22; Titus 1:5-7; Acts 20:17; Acts 20:28

sections.b: 1 Timothy gives the only list of qualities for deacons in the New Testament: serious, honest, not given to wine or greedy, holding the faith with a clean conscience, tested first, husbands of one wife, good household leaders. In the middle stands "Women likewise" (3:11), read either as deacons' wives or as women deacons, like Phoebe (Romans 16:1). Chrysostom took them as deaconesses. Pliny's letter to Trajan mentions two slave women "who were called ministrae" in Bithynia (Letters 10.96.8); the Latin means female attendants, and whether it names a church office is debated.

The longest passage on widows in the New Testament. Families must support their own widows (5:4, 8, 16); the church supports widows who are truly alone and devoted to prayer (5:3, 5); widows over sixty with a record of good works can be enrolled on a list, apparently with a pledge (5:9-12); younger widows should remarry (5:14). The rules answer a strain on the church's resources and a problem with idle young widows going from house to house.

sections.h: "Forbidding marriage" and the husband of one wife
sections.b: 1 Timothy calls the teaching that forbids marriage a teaching of demons (4:1-3), wants younger widows to marry (5:14), and requires overseers and deacons to be "the husband of one wife" (3:2, 12). The churches draw different conclusions: Latin Catholic discipline asks most priests to be celibate while Eastern churches ordain married men; Protestant churches allow ministers to marry; the Orthodox Church does not ordain the remarried. The card on chapter 3 sets them out.

The letter defends marriage against teachers who forbade it (4:3), and treats a good household as a qualification for church leadership (3:4-5, 12). "The husband of one wife" (3:2) and "the wife of one husband" (5:9) are read as rules against polygamy, against remarriage, or for faithfulness in marriage. Younger widows are told to marry (5:14), unlike the advice of 1 Corinthians 7:39-40.

sections.h: "He wants everyone to be saved" (1 Timothy 2:4)
sections.b: 1 Timothy 2:4, with 2:6 ("a ransom on behalf of all") and 4:10 ("Savior of all people, most of all of believers"), is a key text for those who hold that God's saving will reaches every person. Augustine read "all" as "every sort of men," and Calvin as "classes of men"; Chrysostom and Wesley read it of every person. The card on 1 Timothy 2 gives the churches' views.

The letter uses "save" and "Savior" often: Christ came "to save sinners" (1:15); God is "our Savior" who wants all to be saved (2:3-4) and "Savior of all people, most of all of believers" (4:10). It also speaks of a woman "saved through the bearing of children" (2:15) and of Timothy saving himself and his hearers by holding to the teaching (4:16). These last two show the word's range: rescue, keeping safe, and the final salvation that faithfulness leads to.

"one also is the mediator between God and humans: Christ Jesus, himself human" (1 Timothy 2:5). The Augsburg Confession (21) cites it against calling on the saints, and the Westminster Confession and the Second London Baptist Confession say worship is offered "nor in the mediation of any other but of Christ alone" (Westminster 21.2; London 22.2, which cites this verse). The Orthodox Confession of Dositheus confesses Christ "the only mediator" and still calls the saints intercessors (Decree 8). The Catholic Church cites it too, teaching that Mary's and the saints' prayers depend wholly on Christ's mediation and neither add to it nor take from it (Lumen Gentium 60-62). The same chapter asks believers to pray for one another and for all people (2:1), which both sides read in their favor.

sections.h: The pillar of the truth and the deposit (1 Timothy)
sections.b: 1 Timothy calls the church "a pillar and a firm base for the truth" (3:15) and tells Timothy to "guard the deposit" (6:20). It calls a saying of Jesus "Scripture" beside Deuteronomy (5:18) and commands the public reading of Scripture (4:13). Catholic teaching cites 3:15 for the church's role in guarding the faith (Catechism 171), and the Orthodox Confession of Dositheus cites it for the church's witness, "not of inferior authority to that of the Divine Scriptures" (Decree 2). Protestant confessions make Scripture the judge of the church's teaching (Westminster Confession 1.10; Formula of Concord, Rule and Norm).

sections.h: Godliness, contentment and the love of money
sections.b: Godliness with contentment is great gain (6:6); we brought nothing into the world (6:7); those who want to be rich fall into a trap (6:9); "A root of every kind of evil is the love of money" (6:10). The rich are not told to give everything away but to hope in God and be rich in good works (6:17-19). Overseers and deacons must be free from the love of money and from shameful profit (3:3, 8).

common: "Money is the root of all evil" is a common misquotation; the verse says the love of money is a root of every kind of evil.

sections.b: Overseers must not sit long over wine and deacons must not be devoted to much wine (3:3, 8), yet Timothy is told to stop drinking only water and take a little wine for his health (5:23). The verse became a battleground when the temperance movement turned against all alcohol; in 1869 Thomas Welch, a Methodist communion steward in Vineland, New Jersey, began bottling unfermented grape juice because serving wine at Communion troubled him.

1 Timothy names "slave dealers" among the lawbreakers (1:10; the KJV's "menstealers"), echoing the death penalty for stealing a person (Exodus 21:16). It also tells slaves to honor their masters so that God's name is not slandered, and those with believing masters to serve them better because they are brothers (6:1-2). The two passages stand side by side in the letter, and both were cited in the slavery debates of later centuries.

The second of the two places where Paul's letters use arsenokoitai, "men who lie with males" (1 Corinthians 6:9; 1 Timothy 1:10). In 1 Timothy it stands in a list of lawbreakers, between "those who commit sexual sin" and "slave dealers"; many commentators see the list as following the Ten Commandments, which would place it under "do not commit adultery," while others find that pattern loose. The note on 1 Corinthians 6:9 gives the readings of the word.

sections.h: "The law is a good thing" (1 Timothy 1:7-11)
sections.b: The false teachers want to be "teachers of the law" without understanding it (1:7). Paul answers that the law is good if used lawfully: it is aimed not at the righteous but at lawbreakers (1:8-10), in a list many commentators read as following the Ten Commandments. The letter also quotes the law as Scripture for paying elders (5:18, quoting Deuteronomy 25:4) and uses its rule of two or three witnesses (5:19).

Many commentators read the list in 1 Timothy 1:9-10 against the Ten Commandments: from "those who kill their fathers or kill their mothers" to "people who swear falsely" it would follow the second half in order (parents, murder, adultery and sexual sin, stealing people, false witness), with the first terms (lawless, ungodly, unholy) answering to the commandments about God. Bengel and Ellicott saw the order of the Decalogue here; the Expositor's Greek Testament argued against it, since the fit is uneven and nothing stands for coveting.

"For Adam was shaped first, and Eve after him. And Adam was not fooled" (1 Timothy 2:13-14). The letter reads Genesis 2-3 for the order of creation and the woman's deception, using the verbs of the Greek Genesis ("shaped," Genesis 2:7; "fooled," Genesis 3:13). How much weight the argument bears in the rule about women teaching is the center of the debate.

1 Timothy 2:14 says that the woman, not Adam, was deceived, while Romans 5:12 says sin entered the world "through one man." The two are not in conflict for most readers: Adam sinned knowingly, Eve was misled. Chrysostom drew from it that "the woman taught the man once"; modern readers often take it as a warning about deception by false teachers (4:1).

sections.h: The church at Ephesus in 1 Timothy
sections.b: 1 Timothy is set in Ephesus (1:3) and shows a large, established church: households, wealthy patrons and slaves, many widows, paid elders, deacons, and teachers who had gone wrong, as Paul had warned the Ephesian elders in Acts 20:29-30. Theories that tie 2:11-15 to the cult of Artemis have been argued both ways (the Kroegers; Baugh; Glahn).

The letter gives their marks: myths and endless genealogies (1:4), wanting to be teachers of the law (1:7), forbidding marriage and foods (4:3), arguments about words (6:4), teaching for profit (6:5), and "the knowledge that wrongly bears that name" (6:20). Hymenaeus and Alexander are named (1:20). Readers identify them as Jewish-Christian speculators, early Gnostics or ascetics, or a mixture.

sections.h: Handed over to Satan; correcting elders
sections.b: 1 Timothy has two kinds of discipline. Hymenaeus and Alexander are "handed over to Satan" so that they will learn not to blaspheme (1:20), as in 1 Corinthians 5:5. Elders are protected from accusations without two or three witnesses, but those who keep sinning are to be corrected in front of all (5:19-21), without favoritism.

The only mention of Pilate in Paul's letters: Christ Jesus "bore witness to the good confession in front of Pontius Pilate" (1 Timothy 6:13). The Greek may also mean "in the time of Pontius Pilate." The verse holds up Jesus' testimony at his trial as the model for Timothy's own confession.

The church's prayer is to include "every person," kings and those in high office, so that believers can live quiet lives (2:1-2); the reason is that God wants all to be saved (2:4). Men are to pray with raised, holy hands, without anger (2:8). Widows devoted to prayer night and day are honored (5:5).

Under pagan emperors, the church is told to pray "for kings and for all who hold high office, so that we can spend calm and quiet lives" (2:2), in line with Jeremiah 29:7 and Romans 13:1-7. Praying for the ruler, rather than to him, let Christians show loyalty without worshiping the emperor.

sections.h: "Every created thing God made is good" (1 Timothy 4:3-5)
sections.b: Against teachers who ordered people to keep away from certain foods, 1 Timothy appeals to creation: everything God made is good, and nothing is to be refused if received with thanks, since God's word and prayer make it holy (4:3-5). This follows Mark 7:19, Romans 14:14 and 1 Corinthians 10:25-26.

sections.h: A ransom on behalf of all (1 Timothy 2:6)
sections.b: "He gave himself as a ransom on behalf of all" (1 Timothy 2:6) recasts Jesus' saying in Mark 10:45, "to give his life as a ransom in place of many." The word antilytron stresses exchange, and "on behalf of all" ties the ransom to God's will that all be saved (2:4).

Deacons must hold "the mystery of the faith" (3:9), and the letter then quotes it in the form of a hymn: "the mystery of godliness is great: He was made visible in the flesh ..." (3:16). The mystery here is Christ himself, made known.
1 Timothy speaks of Christ's return as his "appearing" (epiphaneia, 6:14), which God will show "at its own set times" (6:15). The Pastorals prefer this word to Paul's earlier parousia, "coming."

1 Timothy presents Paul as the first and model case of mercy: once "a man who blasphemed, persecuted and abused," now an apostle and "a teacher of the Gentiles" (1:13; 2:7). He has left Timothy in Ephesus and gone to Macedonia (1:3), and hopes to come back soon (3:14). Whether this is Paul himself or a portrait drawn by a later follower is set out on the topic page on the Pastoral Letters.
